items.summary: The macroscopic capabilities of intelligent systems arise from the local interactions of many simple units. When such systems are deployed in the real world, their behaviour must nevertheless be constrained, leaving designers caught between releasing adaptability and preventing loss of control, yet without formal tools to resolve the dilemma. This paper proposes a unified research program for controlled emergence that restates this tension as a pair of dual problems: the forward problem explains macroscopic behaviour from local rules, and the inverse problem solves for controllable rules and readout mechanisms from a desired target. We take an augmented quintuple as the formal object shared by both ends, and decompose ``engineering'' into three independently measurable coordinates: controllability, reproducibility, and degree of formalizability. On this basis we give three testable working hypotheses (critical scale; the cooperation and trade-off between constraint and adaptability; minimal constraint) and one feasibility criterion, which reduce inverse design from unconstrained optimization to interval checking. The program takes explicit failure boundaries as its premise, does not pursue complete control, and always preserves the system's room for self-organization. The reduced pilot experiment attached to this paper serves only to verify the executability of the research protocol and does not constitute a statistical test of the working hypotheses. This design language generalizes to multi-agent artificial intelligence, the industrial internet, and emergency response systems, all of which must confront emergence and controllability at once.
items.title: The Forward/Inverse Duality of Controlled Emergence:A Computational Design Program from Explanation to Engineering

items.summary: Model--harness co-evolution has emerged as a prominent paradigm for recursive self-improving (RSI) agents, jointly evolving their execution scaffolds and intrinsic capabilities. We study the persistent yet often overlooked brain--body mismatch problem in this paradigm, where an evolving harness (body) demands behaviors its model (brain) has not learned or restricts capabilities it already possesses. We introduce CoEvo-RSI, a RSI framework that advances model--harness co-evolution through agent-driven, bidirectional historical inheritance. Drawing on a shared evolutionary archive and execution feedback, a meta-agent coordinates harness development from historical designs with model checkpoint selection or merging and subsequent adaptation under the selected harness, aligning inherited capabilities with evolving execution requirements to reduce brain--body mismatch. Using only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on its own rejection-sampled trajectories, CoEvo-RSI makes Qwen3.5-9B competitive with larger models across diverse vertical applications, including multi-agent failure attribution, role-aware text-to-SQL, and smart-home instruction following. It surpasses DeepSeek-V4-Pro on TraceElephant (+14.16 agent accuracy) and GLM-5.3 on HomeBench VM (+4.90 success rate), underscoring the need for brain--body alignment and the potential of bidirectional historical inheritance to advance agent co-evolution.
items.title: CoEvo-RSI: When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?

items.summary: Open radio access network (O-RAN) enables a multi-vendor ecosystem that accelerates xApp development for near-real-time (RT) network management. However, this openness shifts a combinatorial coordination burden to the Non-RT layer, where rApp policies compose xApps from a growing catalog to realize operator intents. Coexisting intents further compound this challenge, as conflicts may arise among xApp actions, rApp policies, and their cross-layer interactions. To maximize intent admission while maintaining key performance indicator (KPI) compliance across incoming and incumbent intents, we propose a large language model-based Multi-Agentic AI framework. A Reasoning Agent screens candidate xApps against KPI contracts and produces a joint intent admission and xApp assignment decision. On post-deployment KPI violations, a Diagnosis Agent identifies the root causes of failure, labels the conflict mechanism, and guides the Reasoning Agent in subsequent attempts. Experimental results show that the framework based on GPT-OSS 120B achieves 28.6% more KPI-compliant cases and admits over 15* as many incoming intents as state-of-the-art baselines. Under the Qwen 72B variant, Diagnosis increases compliant cases by 50.0%, quadruples admitted intents, and reduces deployment attempts by 32.6%. A live deployment conforming to O-RAN specifications further validates the feasibility of the proposed solution for conflict-aware rApp policy orchestration in real networks.
items.title: Multi-Agentic AI for Intent-Driven and Conflict-Aware rApp Policy Orchestration in Open RAN

items.summary: Commit messages provide records of code changes and help developers understand and maintain software. To reduce the manual effort involved in writing them, commit message generation (CMG) approaches automatically generate commit messages that describe code changes in natural language. Existing CMG approaches generally treat CMG as a standalone task and optimize generated messages primarily for similarity to developer-written references. However, this objective may not properly reflect the practical usefulness of generated commit messages. This limitation matters in current AI-assisted software engineering workflows, where commit messages are used as shared information to serve different software engineering activities. To fill this gap, we propose TraceMsg, which uses issue-commit traceability, a representative software engineering activity, to guide commit message generation. TraceMsg is a collaborative multi-agent framework that coordinates message generation, traceability reasoning, and feedback-guided refinement, allowing generated messages to serve traceability while using reasoning feedback to guide issue-conditioned refinement. We evaluate TraceMsg on six open-source projects. The experimental results show that TraceMsg achieves an average Hit@1 of 0.893 and an MRR of 0.911, improving Hit@1 and MRR by 13.16% and 38.75%, respectively, over the best baseline for each metric.
items.title: Beyond Similarity-Based Generation: Guiding Commit Message Generation with Issue-Commit Traceability

items.summary: Post-training compression of pretrained medical segmentation models commonly uses quantization, pruning, or distillation to reduce model size and computational cost. Existing medical segmentation quantization studies mainly evaluate Dice, model size, memory, and latency, but this is incomplete for safety-critical use because compressed models should also preserve uncertainty signals that indicate unreliable predictions. We study this problem in compressed MRI/CT segmentation and formalize why Dice can remain stable while uncertainty changes. Motivated by this failure mode, we propose score-guided aggregate-validated mixed precision (SGAV-MP), a post-training compression framework that selects layer precisions under reliability constraints. SGAV-MP ranks quantization actions with a compact benefit-risk score and accepts them only after full-model reliability validation on a calibration set. Across five 2D backbones and three 3D benchmarks, SGAV-MP preserves FP32-level Dice and high uncertainty-map agreement, achieving $3.59\times$--$7.8\times$ compression in 2D and $4.73\times$--$7.82\times$ in 3D. We also report backend-supported TensorRT deployment measurements separately to distinguish runtime execution from reliability-preserving storage compression.
items.title: Reliability-Preserving Compression for Deployable Medical Image Segmentation

items.summary: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) trains policies for open-ended generation with natural-language criteria as rewards, but these rewards can become ineffective as training progresses. We identify two failure modes. Under non-discriminative rewards, scores collapse to uniformly low or high values due to insufficient exploration or a mismatch between task difficulty and policy capability. Under spurious rewards, higher scores do not correspond to better responses. Both reflect a training configuration whose task sampling, exploration, and evaluation stay fixed as the policy evolves. We introduce HarnessRL, a training-time harness that co-evolves with the policy through three interfaces for task sampling, rollout guidance, and rubric criteria. HarnessRL maintains a training-time memory from which a harness evolver retrieves within-task history and cross-task evidence. Using this evidence, the evolver attributes each reward failure to the interface whose update can address it. It then runs a proposer and just-in-time critic loop in which the critic accepts a candidate update only after measuring its effect on the current frozen policy, returning rejected candidates for revision. We also curate Rubric-Mix-10k, a five-domain training and evaluation suite for open-ended RL across medical, science, writing, role-play, and instruction-following tasks. On Rubric-Mix-10k, HarnessRL outperforms the strongest baselines by 2.8 to 3.1 points across both 4B and 9B model scales and nearly halves the training steps to its best checkpoint. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Tongyi-ConvAI/Qwen-Character/tree/main/HarnessRL.
items.title: HarnessRL: Co-Evolving Policies with a Just-in-Time Training Harness for Open-Ended RL

items.summary: Recent research-level physics-reasoning benchmarks for LLMs reveal a failure mode that lies not in knowledge or execution, but in modeling the world being reasoned about. Models often silently alter given quantities, fabricate laws, or inject unstated assumptions to force a problem into familiar patterns, and then reason inside this corrupted world. We define this premise-level divergence as modeling drift: the gap between a model's internal axiomatic world model (AWM) and the true physical world specified in the problem. Although RLVR and PRM have yielded substantial gains in mathematics and code, their reward shapes do not directly supervise world modeling in axiomatic domains such as physics. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Axiomatic World Modeling (RLAWM), which optimizes the policy by penalizing divergence between its inferred axiomatic world model and the true physics world. RLAWM probes physics reasoning at two hierarchical levels (modeling and solving), each scored by a physically grounded reward. The modeling reward targets abstract knowledge formulation, evaluating whether the model captures the true axiomatic world before attempting calculation. The solving reward targets instantiated knowledge reasoning, checking whether the model's concrete derivation remains consistent with the axiomatic world. This two-level structure separates what world the model believes it is reasoning in from how it reasons within that world. The framework operates exclusively during training, with no extra cost during inference. RLAWM improves performance by up to +12.2 points on PhysReason and +5.2 on PHYSICS over the baseline. It also generalizes zero-shot across difficulty, source, and domain, with a 2.45x gain and +10 points over the strongest baseline on olympiad-level physics and math.
items.title: Axiomatic World Modeling for Physics Reasoning

items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are trained through multi-stage pipelines over heterogeneous data sources, yet developers lack a principled way to pinpoint the specific data responsible for an observed behavior. This lack of observability reduces debugging to reactive patching and makes failures prone to recur under distribution shift or subsequent model updates. To address this limitation, we propose DebugLM, a framework that equips LLMs with built-in data provenance, enabling them to explicitly trace the origins of their behaviors to specific training data sources. Specifically, the model learns to associate its responses with unique provenance tags that indicate the responsible dataset, empowering developers to precisely identify where undesirable behaviors are learned. Building on this capability, DebugLM further supports targeted test-time remediation, enabling developers to selectively trigger targeted refusal for specified data sources without retraining or modifying model parameters. Experiments demonstrate that DebugLM provides accurate behavior tracing in multi-stage training pipelines and effective test-time remediation while preserving the general utility of the model.
items.title: DebugLM: Learning Traceable Training Data Provenance for LLMs

items.summary: Archival deposit accompanying A Controlled Audit of a Negative Result: Training Recipe, H.264 Compression Levels and a Frequency-Stream Deepfake Detector , under review at IEEE Access (revision 1). This is version v2.0.2 of the deposit; it goes with release v2.0.2 of the repository. This controlled, self-audited study tests one frequency-based design for compression-robust deepfake detection: CAFRL, which adds block-DCT and FFT-phase streams with compression-conditioned band attention, and an adversarial compression-invariance loss, to an EfficientNet-B0 face backbone. Five separate findings follow. (1) Under the registered rule, CAFRL as specified scored 3.66 AUC points below a backbone-matched EfficientNet-B0 at CRF 40 (paired, one seed). (2) After the audit found eight defects, the control's training recipe recovered 3.96 points for CAFRL's own components (post-audit pre-specified); in a one-seed ablation reverting changes singly, only the backbone learning rate gave an interval excluding zero. (3) At that recipe, these untuned frequency-stream implementations showed no detectable difference from the spatial controls at two feature widths (post-audit pre-specified), yet a standalone frequency head scored 85.27 test-split AUC points at CRF 40 at the selected checkpoints (exploratory). (4) Restoring the adversarial loss at that recipe made no detectable difference in a registered test (0.87 points, Holm-adjusted p = 0.084); the estimator stayed accurate at the selected checkpoints. (5) In registered three-seed tests, real H.264 training levels beat PSNR-matched JPEG versions of the same frames by 7.48 points at CRF 40 (averaged over CRF-40 exposure), and CRF-40-level data added 1.88 points averaged over codec; flat robustness was measured within the trained levels. CAFRL numbers use EMA weights. Evidence: FaceForensics++-family, GAN-era, single-pass H.264 compression. The repository — https://github.com/Capta1n-n9m0/cafrl-negative — holds the per-video model scores, the decision rules frozen before the runs they adjudicate, every run's configuration and validation curve, the evaluation and statistical harness, the face-crop and re-encode pipeline, the self-audit record with its defect ledger, and two claims maps that give the artifact and method for each reported value row by row. Its tagged tree (v2.0.2) is included here as cafrl-negative-v2.0.2.tar.gz . This version holds: cafrl-negative-v2.0.2.tar.gz — the repository at tag v2.0.2 (new). <run>.best.pt — 26 frozen model checkpoints (2.7 GB in all), one file per run: the best.pt (best mean validation AUC) of each run added in revision 1, with checkpoints-r1-manifest.json giving each one's run, architecture, arm, training protocol, augmentation policy, seed, selected epoch, selection metric and SHA-256 (carried unchanged from v2.0.1, first deposited in v2.0.0; no best_valloss.pt ). The v2.0.0 release notes call this payload checkpoints-r1.tar ; the deposit holds the same 26 checkpoints as separate files. checkpoints.tar — 37 frozen model checkpoints (6.0 GB), every best*.pt of the 27 v1.0.0 runs, with checkpoints-manifest.json (carried unchanged from v2.0.1, first deposited in v1.0.0). crop-coordinates.tar.zst — 48,294 per-video face-crop records: the frames selected, the bounding boxes, the five-point landmarks and the alignment settings. Given the source corpora, obtained under your own data-use agreement, these regenerate the exact crops the models were trained and evaluated on (carried unchanged from v2.0.1, first deposited in v1.0.0; this version adds no crop coordinates). SHA256SUMS (every file above, the carried ones included) and README-DEPOSIT.md . The v2.0.1 source tarball stays in the v2.0.1 record and is not part of this version. No dataset media is redistributed here or in the repository. FaceForensics++, DeepFakeDetection and Celeb-DF v2 are released by their authors under signed agreements that do not per
items.title: Artifacts for "A Controlled Audit of a Negative Result: Training Recipe, H.264 Compression Levels and a Frequency-Stream Deepfake Detector"

items.summary: Multi-agent scientific discovery with large language models raises a coupled learning problem: research assignments determine both which experiments are pursued and the experiences from which agents adapt. We introduce MELD, a unified hierarchical test-time training framework that jointly adapts a team-level Coordinator policy and agent-level individual Scientist policies within a single discovery process. The Coordinator generates a joint portfolio of search branches and research directives over a shared derivation tree, while Scientists develop hypotheses and execution plans implemented by a shared frozen Executor. Both levels receive alternating GRPO-style parameter updates under a shared smooth best-of-budget objective, allowing team organization and individual research behavior to co-evolve in a recursive self-improvement loop. Our analysis establishes objective alignment for the hierarchy, characterizes conditions for coordination gains over independent parallel discovery and the first-order benefit of private adaptation, and derives a finite-budget regret bound for adapted models. On 22 MLGym and MLE-bench tasks, MELD is best on 20 of them and achieves the highest aggregate normalized scores on MLGym, using a 4B backbone for coordination and research. Most baselines use proprietary Scientists, and all systems share one frozen Executor.
items.title: MELD: Recursive Self-Improvement via Hierarchical Coordination for Multi-Agent Scientific Discovery

items.summary: AI agents are growing more capable and persistent, and are being deployed in ever larger numbers. As more start collaborating, AI control measures must remain effective when they covertly collude on a harmful objective. We introduce MiniLab, a synthetic series of live services and codebases (5 interconnected services, 249 benign tasks, 8 attack objectives), adapted from internal AI deployment infrastructure. We demonstrate distributed attacks, in which different agents carry out separate attack fragments, and how their covertness evades frontier monitors when reading their trajectories individually. We show how distributed attacks spread across diverse contexts and harmful objectives through 16 human-optimized attacks (weight exfiltration, unmonitored rogue deployment, permission elevation, and more). A frontier monitor, GPT-5.6 Sol, reading each agent separately flags only 7% of successful distributed attacks, compared with 87% when a single agent carries out the same side task. Individual attacks can also be composed into longer attack sequences toward a greater loss-of-control outcome, without any individual agent being flagged. Finally, we tested whether models can plan these covert attacks: even with execution and monitor feedback, the best model-planned attacks succeed covertly against a single-trajectory GPT-5.6 Sol monitor in at most 25% of executions, compared with 80% for human-crafted plans, though this may scale with model capabilities. By turning worst-case coordinated attacks into reproducible red-team cases, our work provides a foundation for preventing locally benign agent actions from accumulating into system-level loss of control.
items.title: Red-Teaming Multi-Agent Attacks for Loss-of-Control Risks

items.summary: A market maker provides liquidity by quoting prices to buy and sell an asset, earning the spread while managing inventory risk. We study market makers trained with multi-agent reinforcement learning on prediction markets, specifically Polymarket, whose thin order books pose distinct challenges. Three challenges underpin this research: adverse selection may cause a policy trained on real data to stop quoting; the consequences of a quote can arrive many steps after the action; and prediction-market L2 data does not identify individual orders needed for simulation. We address these challenges by reconstructing order-level LOBSTER-format data from Polymarket and training agents in JaxMARL-HFT on 417 real markets. We enrich the baseline market maker's observation space with the book and recent flow, redesign its actions and inventory controls, and propose a cooperative multi-agent decomposition into a quoter and a risk manager trained using recurrent Independent Proximal Policy Optimisation (IPPO) with RNN policies. We investigate reward shaping, particularly reward blending and post-fill markout, to mitigate credit-assignment difficulties between the agents. Our redesigned single-agent market maker quotes more frequently and incurs smaller held-out losses than the retrained JaxMARL-HFT baseline, although the contributions of jointly changed observations, actions and risk constraints are not separately identified. Decomposition alone performs poorly; careful reward design substantially improves the desk relative to the unshaped split and yields our best result. Models are evaluated on realised end-of-episode portfolio value on held-out markets. None establishes positive average portfolio value in periodic held-out evaluation, and each configuration was trained with one seed. The environment, data and protocol lay a foundation for makers that quote many linked markets at once.
items.title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Market Making on Prediction-Market Order Books

items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to refactor source files, but file-local evaluations do not reveal changes to contracts, dependencies, or caller assumptions affecting repository adoption. To address this gap, we conduct 1,500 generation attempts across 150 production files from 15 open-source Java repositories, five LLM configurations, and two dependency-aware generation conditions: single-prompt refactoring and LangGraph-based multi-agent refactoring. Of these attempts, 1,455 yield complete candidates eligible for analysis. We evaluate these candidates using local changes, repository-facing structural indicators, detected caller impact, the behavioural-equivalence indicator, and available test evidence, and categorize them as Low-risk, Review-needed, High Contract/Dependency Risk, or Inconclusive. The results show that 1,365 candidates (93.8%) are classified as High Contract/Dependency Risk, whereas 106 (7.3%) have at least one detected broken downstream caller and 290 (19.9%) have a false behavioural-equivalence indicator; only eight satisfy the Low-risk criteria. Within the reason-covered subset, the High-risk rate decreases under more conservative dependency-delta thresholds, while 60 of the 65 candidates with conclusive targeted-test outcomes pass, including 50 classified as High risk. Paired analyses of 705 complete pairs identify no statistically significant generation-condition difference in the principal risk indicators, although model configurations differ in specific detected risk channels. These findings suggest that practitioners should treat LLM-generated refactorings as candidates requiring staged repository-level verification, while future research should validate screening and extraction precision and strengthen compilation, behavioural, and coordinated multi-file verification.
items.title: When LLM-Generated Refactorings Ripple: An Empirical Study of Repository Adoption Readiness

items.summary: Multi-agent approaches have been investigated recently as a means of improving the scalability of reinforcement learning for neural combinatorial optimization. Existing methods assume that all problem instance information is known upfront. However, real-world problems are often dynamic: relevant information is progressively revealed as the agents take actions (e.g., arriving at an edge in a routing problem only to discover it is untraversable). In such cases, existing methods fail to coordinate agents to explore and exploit the progressively revealed information. To address the arising coordination challenge, we introduce PACT (Plan-Augmented Coordination via Trace-graphs). PACT augments the environment graph with auxiliary nodes representing the plans of agents, which are connected to the resource nodes to indicate future dependencies. The proposed message-passing scheme over the augmented graph grounds inter-agent coordination in the environment and enables proactive, rather than reactive, conflict resolution. We show that PACT improves solution quality in dynamic problems relative to baselines and exhibits the best transfer to larger instances on which, remarkably, it outperforms centralized oracles with privileged access to instance uncertainty.
items.title: PACT: Plan-Augmented Coordination via Trace-Graphs for Dynamic Multi-Agent Combinatorial Optimization

items.summary: As automated research is increasingly adopted for writing papers, automated review has become a critical link between paper generation and quality control. However, existing methods largely rely on single-model feedback or simple review aggregation, failing to explicitly model expert responsibilities or collective deliberation in actual peer reviews, which limits effective cross-examination and reliable decision-making. Therefore, we formulate paper review as a computational modeling problem of peer review mechanisms and propose RoundtableReview, a deliberative multi-agent framework for enhancing automated research. RoundtableReview structures each paper into eight semantic slots and coordinates six academic and industry reviewers with complementary perspectives, retrieval sources, and specialized responsibilities. Through independent assessment, cross-examination, roundtable deliberation, dynamically weighted voting, and chair synthesis, the framework generates evidence-based and traceable feedback. Experiments on two automated research backbones show that the method improves paper quality in both backbones and outperforms baselines in automatic and human evaluations with fewer comments.
items.title: Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review

items.summary: Recent test-time scaling methods improve model performance by increasing inference-time compute. One practical form of this is parallel scaling, where a model samples multiple independent reasoning streams and aggregates their answers using methods like voting, reranking, or verification. While effective, this approach leaves the streams uncoordinated, and a discovery made in one rollout cannot influence any other. Multi-Sequence Verifiers jointly score candidate answers after generation, but the reasoning streams remain independent during inference. ParScale takes a step toward model-internal parallel scaling by learning to aggregate multiple forward passes, but its streams still do not exchange information while processing a sequence. We introduce BatchParScale, an attention mechanism that allows parallel streams to exchange information through a small set of communication positions. We evaluate BatchParScale on a new Parallel Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval benchmark and in pretraining, fine-tuning, and cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. Across these settings, BatchParScale outperforms ParScale on language-model loss and remains competitive on coordination-sensitive MARL tasks. Masked pretraining runs beat an unmasked single-sequence baseline despite local sequence corruption, and LoRA fine-tuning shows the mechanism can be added to a pretrained Transformer. At the same time, fact retrieval performance for pretrained and finetuned BatchParScale models remains unclear.
items.title: BatchParScale: Sparse Batch-Mixing for Sequence Models

items.summary: Developing coordination policies for complex multi-agent systems relies on either labor-intensive algorithm design or opaque task-specific reinforcement learning. With recent advances in autonomous coding agents, we show that policy search directly in code space offers a compelling third path that combines automated optimization with explicit interpretability. We investigate a human-directed workflow in which coding agents iteratively propose, implement, evaluate, diagnose, and eventually refine algorithms guided by simulation feedback and explicit correctness verification. We conducted two case studies and found that this workflow robustly outperformed any manually engineered solutions. On a challenging map in the 2024 League of Robot Runners competition, a two-day search discovered a policy that exceeds the stronger locally reproduced competition entry by 35.0% on the densest instance and generalizes to unseen map instances. In simulated real-world warehouses with irregular lanes, continuous robot geometry, and asynchronous motion, a week-long search discovered an entirely new class of multi-agent pathfinding algorithm that outperforms a calibrated proprietary solution in throughput by 58.9%. Under stated assumptions, we further prove that the new algorithm is collision-free and completes, in finite time, every accepted goal that is not withdrawn or replaced. Together, the studies show that policy search in code space powered by state-of-the-art coding agents offers a highly competitive path to building real engineering solutions that are both effective and analytically tractable.
items.title: Policy Search in Code Space for Multi-Agent Pathfinding

items.summary: Serverless computing is increasingly used to run complex DAG workflows across diverse applications, and individual function execution times have grown to support them, pushing workflow makespans to hours. Open-source serverless platforms, deployed on a pool of VMs, typically use on-demand instances, and their cost increases with the makespan. Spot instances are far cheaper, but a preemption is likely before the workflow finishes. A preemption at a fan-out node or a task feeding a fan-in node stalls every parallel branch, cascading a single preemption into a workflow-wide failure. Prior systems address this challenge by migrating high-impact tasks to reliable, non-spot resources, sacrificing spot's cost advantage. We present FaaSpot, a serverless workflow execution system that runs every workflow task on spot instances with no on-demand fallback. Our key insight is that cascade-prone positions are determined by the DAG's topology and can be identified before execution. Therefore, FaaSpot analyzes the workflow DAG once at submission time and classifies each task by the impact of its preemption. Selective checkpointing, survival-aware scaling, and lineage-based retry then act on this single classification, with no runtime coordination. We evaluate FaaSpot on a trace-driven spot emulator with eight DAG workflows against four state-of-the-art baselines. FaaSpot completes 89.03% of runs at $0.018 per successful run, 21pp (percentage points) above the average baseline success rate and at a lower cost per success than every baseline, while reducing mean latency by 2.3x.
items.title: FaaSpot: Fault-Tolerant Serverless Workflow Execution on Spot Instances

items.summary: Small Language Models with quantisation and parameter-efficient adaptation are widely offered as the route to multilingual AI under compute constraints, and their efficiency is almost always reported as a single memory figure. We show that this figure is measured in English and does not transfer. Across a 131k-sentence corpus spanning eleven Indic scripts, TinyLlama-1.1B's tokeniser emits 1.34 subword tokens per Latin-script word and 22.60 per Kannada word. This is not inefficiency; it is absence. Its vocabulary contains 0% of Odia's codepoints, 1% of Telugu's and 2% of Kannada's, and for five of eleven scripts the measured fertility sits at the UTF-8 byte-fallback ceiling, on Odia at 99.6% of it, with 93.6% of emitted tokens being raw bytes. Because SentencePiece byte fallback never raises an unknown-token marker, this failure is entirely silent: TinyLlama's UNK rate is 0.0% on every script, including the one it reads as bytes. We further show that low fertility can indicate the opposite of efficiency: mBERT posts its best score anywhere (1.10 tokens/word, on Odia) while discarding 87.9% of the text as UNK. MuRIL, an Indic-vocabulary encoder with a fifth of TinyLlama's parameters, reads every script at 1.23-2.26 tokens/word with zero UNK and zero byte fallback. The binding constraint is the vocabulary, not the parameter count. The consequence is concrete: on a 2048-token context window, the same model gives an English user 1,528 words of usable context and a Kannada user 91.
items.title: Efficiency Measured in English: Tokeniser Coverage Bounds Small Language Models on Indic Scripts

items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate Verus contracts for Rust programs together with the proofs that establish them. Yet verifier acceptance, the common measure of success, shows only that the implementation satisfies the generated contract, so it leaves open whether the contract captures the intended behavior. Assessing specification generation therefore requires an evaluation methodology, not a single metric. We present VerusEval, a framework that evaluates generated contracts along six dimensions, including Verus-native checks for semantic triviality, validated input-output (I/O) suites, and contract equivalence, and that relates them so that the strength and blind spots of each become measurable. Evaluating 13,716 artifacts from four workflows, five LLMs, and two prompting settings on 762 tasks, we find that acceptance overstates quality: only 42.3\% of the accepted artifacts complete all three semantic checks without a flag, and across workflows and models, higher acceptance does not consistently come with more correct contracts. I/O evaluation rejects 23.6\% of the accepted artifacts, yet only 63.2\% of those that pass it are proved equivalent. Of the accepted artifacts flagged by contract comparison, 84.1\% have a rejected completeness obligation, and the direction of a failure prioritizes inspection of the generated contract or the reference; it does not by itself establish which artifact is defective. Screening and review further identify 36 candidate defects among 61 selected reference contracts, and repairing one of them makes 10 of its 11 failing artifacts equivalent. Based on these findings, we derive four actionable lessons for evaluation, generation, and benchmark maintenance.
items.title: VerusEval: Evaluating LLM-Generated Verus Specifications Beyond Verifier Acceptance

items.summary: Evaluating an agent's planning ability remains challenging for open-domain tasks, where verifying procedures through execution is often impractical. Existing evaluations typically assess only the final plan and do not distinguish procedural errors such as missing, incorrect, or misordered actions. We introduce STEPBENCH, a benchmark of 6,885 verified procedures crawled from wikiHow across 81 open-domain categories. From each procedure, we derive 5 diagnostic tasks: four with deterministic answers involving withheld, incorrect, or shuffled steps, and one requiring next-step generation. We additionally evaluate full-plan generation to examine how diagnostic performance correlates with end-to-end plan validity. Using the same procedures across tasks lets us directly compare different planning capabilities. For generation, STEPEVAL identifies critical failures that prevent goal completion. Across 14 configurations of 12 models, we find substantial differences across planning capabilities, with step ordering proving the most difficult: the strongest model correctly orders only 63.0% of procedures, dropping to 33.1% for those with nine or more steps. Incorrect-step detection also predicts judged plan validity across models, suggesting a lower-cost alternative for evaluating generation quality. On STEPBENCH-Val, comprising 214 procedures published in 2026, comprehension scores and rankings remain stable, suggesting limited influence from memorisation.
items.title: StebBench: Diagnosing Real-World Procedural Understanding in AI Agents

items.summary: A small justification for a rule-based conclusion may disappear when a source is withdrawn, and multiple derivations need not provide independent evidence. We study minimum-cost certificates that preserve a Horn conclusion under every withdrawal of at most k source domains. Evidence records remain distinct from asserted facts, supporting replicated attestations and overlapping failure dependencies. Transversals of minimal-support footprints characterize robustness and explain why disjoint-proof requirements can reject valid certificates. An exact procedure alternates weighted evidence selection with a source-failure oracle. A rule-closed counterinterpretation yields a globally valid selection cut without enumerating supports or failure scenarios. We prove correctness, finite termination, and cost optimality, establish coNP-completeness of unrestricted verification and NP-completeness of synthesis for every fixed budget, and identify a tractable reachability restriction. Experiments on controlled benchmarks, reachability graphs, and ontology-derived instances demonstrate that our counterinterpretation-guided synthesis achieves up to 92% optimum coverage within practical resource bounds, outperforming scenario expansion and general abduction while confirming the necessity of transversal-based reasoning over proof-packing heuristics.
items.title: Minimum-Cost Robust Evidence Certificates for Horn Reasoning under Correlated Source Failures

items.summary: Distributed LLM serving relies on a global index to locate reusable key-value cache (KVCache) blocks through prefix matching. Losing the index after a crash or restart forces affected requests to recompute existing KVCache on GPUs. Persisting the index restores access after a failure. Existing persistent indexes face a tension between prefix-matching performance and recovery time. A snapshot-backed in-memory index supports fast prefix matching, but rebuilding the full index delays recovery. An on-SSD index avoids this rebuild, but adds storage accesses to prefix matching. Our core insight is that extending a matched prefix over a short span typically requires distinguishing only a few token sequences, suggesting that sparse in-memory routing state may suffice. Prefix matching also accesses block metadata in sequence order, allowing metadata for consecutive blocks to be retrieved together. We present SARP (Sparse Adaptive Routing and Packing), an on-SSD KVCache index for fast recovery and prefix matching. SARP groups consecutive block IDs and metadata into segments to amortize storage accesses across multiple blocks. A compact in-memory routing directory identifies candidate segments using entries at selected block positions. SARP limits segment retrievals and uses compact filters to prioritize candidates with longer potential matches. After retrieval, SARP verifies block IDs against the query and reuses only KVCache blocks covered by the verified prefix. After a restart, SARP restores the sparse routing directory from a snapshot. Across four multi-turn chat and agentic workloads, SARP recovers 8.0x to 77.5x faster than the in-memory index baselines and delivers 1.15x to 66.6x the request throughput of the on-SSD index baselines, while reusing only 0.0030% to 0.029% fewer tokens than exact prefix matching.
items.title: SARP: An On-SSD Index for KVCache with Fast Prefix Matching and Recovery

items.summary: Fault localization (FL) aims to identify code locations responsible for software failures and is commonly evaluated by how accurately it ranks known fault locations. Large language model (LLM) agents are changing program repair and are increasingly used to search and reason over repositories. Although recent LLM-based FL methods have improved localization accuracy, their impact on agentic repair remains unclear. To address this gap, we conduct a systematic empirical study of FL in agentic repair. We evaluate six recent FL methods on SWE-bench Verified and Defects4J with three LLMs under a common repair framework and analyze 16,248 repair trajectories. We also examine gold locations and bug-cause descriptions as forms of FL guidance across different repair contexts. The studied FL methods do not consistently improve repair success, and higher localization accuracy does not consistently lead to larger repair gains. Yet FL guides agents' early search and helps them reach relevant code sooner. Accurate locations can reduce repair token use by up to 39.2\%, but current FL methods often consume more tokens than they save during repair. Experiments with gold guidance suggest that FL has greater potential when bug inputs contain fewer location clues. Providing bug causes can further improve repair success beyond locations alone. We also find that ground truth from a single reference patch does not fully capture the locations used by successful repairs. These findings help clarify the value of FL in agentic repair and inform future work on its design and evaluation.
items.title: From Finding to Fixing: How Useful is Fault Localization for Agentic Program Repair?

items.summary: Version 2.3 of Adversarial Multi-AI Falsification is a bounded case study of AI-assisted scholarly workflow governance. It distinguishes selected public verbatim excerpts and message/line maps from author-reported recovery findings and hashes identifying internal artifacts. The public deposit does not contain the full captured transcripts or executed rubric. Four process-failure types required exclusion or downgrading: semantic drift with unsupported process certification; assignment-scope expansion; prior-task substitution; and unverified or misdescribed legal citations. E2 remains partial. The principal execution/adjudication sequence remains author-reconstructed, and panel unanimity cannot be independently recomputed from the public deposit. The operational proposition remains untested; this revision does not establish it as true. The paper proposes a three-field outcome record and six workflow controls, including a two-turn assignment-echo checkpoint. These are unvalidated design propositions, not demonstrated interventions. This is a case report and protocol demonstration, not a benchmark, product comparison, prevalence estimate or complete reproducibility study. AMAF_v2_3.pdf is the current controlling manuscript, with AMAF_v2_3.docx as its editable counterpart. All seven v2.2 files are retained unchanged as historical records, including the old preparation-candidate manuscript, README, manifest and checksum list. Read 00_README_AMAF_v2_3_RELEASE.txt for the current controlling-version guide; AMAF_v2_3_SHA256SUMS.txt lists this release's file identities. The historical v1.8 paper is retained only for its Section C dual-track summary. No additional private records, new experiment or new empirical validation are released. Generative AI systems were used for structured literature discovery, comparative issue mapping, adversarial review, source-check planning, language editing and revision support. They are not authors. The human author retains responsibility for the sources, interpretations, arguments and conclusions.
items.title: Adversarial Multi-AI Falsification in Research Workflows: A Bounded Case Study of Scope Error, Verification Failure, and Human Adjudication

items.summary: Autonomous clinical-modeling agents can optimize predictive performance while violating conditions that make a model usable. We introduce LeakBench, an executable, guideline-derived audit suite that tests agent decisions for prediction-time leakage, calibration, site-level evaluation, support awareness, and decision-curve net benefit. LeakBench combines a synthetic task with known failure structure and two real-data settings: MIMIC-IV (430k admissions) and governed multi-hospital inpatient record front-page (MHFP) data. Our primary analysis uses reward hacking descriptively, without attributing intent: an agent selects prediction-time-invalid inputs because they improve its validation reward. A deterministic optimizer and every evaluated unconstrained local-model configuration select a fatal leaking feature. In fully logged September 2026 A/B runs, DeepSeek Flash and GPT-6-astra each leak in 10/10 unconstrained runs and 0/10 runs with an explicit admission-time constraint. This contrast is version-sensitive: a blinded Claude/Fable-5.1 chat run does not leak in either condition, while explicit-constraint violations appear only in a historical August 2026 slice lacking raw trajectories. Replacing AUROC with AUPRC does not remove leakage selection. Renaming or disguising the leaking inputs changes neither selection nor provenance-based detection; a name-based filter fails. A deterministic provenance verifier-in-loop removes the leak, making the LLM repair loop defense-in-depth. Specific verifier feedback clears fatal leakage in a hosted agent, and a three-seed ablation finds principle-only feedback clears decision-level defects, though these mitigation results are limited. LeakBench treats trustworthy clinical prediction as a property of an agent's modeling process, not merely its score; it is an audit testbed with known-failure controls, not yet an expert-validated benchmark.
items.title: LeakBench: Auditing Reward Hacking through Prediction-Time Leakage in Clinical Modeling Agents

items.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) learns from pairwise preferences through a logistic objective whose score-difference parameterization follows the Bradley--Terry model. We study how failure of this modeling assumption limits DPO, distinguishing structural misspecification from limited model capacity and finite-sample estimation. Our main contribution is a characterization of structural approximation error through the triangle-curl of the preference log-odds, which vanishes exactly when preferences admit a Bradley--Terry representation. We upper bound the achievable excess logistic risk by a score-class approximation term and a triangle-curl term, and establish a lower bound proportional to triangle-curl under additional boundedness assumptions. For ReLU score models, including clipped models, we derive explicit approximation rates showing that increasing capacity can eliminate the score-approximation term while leaving the structural obstruction unchanged. We further establish finite-sample bounds for clipped empirical risk minimizers that separate network approximation, structural misspecification, and estimation error. We place these results within a surrogate-risk framework by identifying contextual preference accuracy (CPA) as a natural measure of agreement between preference judgments and changes in pairwise probability ratios relative to the reference policy. Standard logistic consistency and calibration results connect DPO's objective to this policy property and transfer our excess-risk upper bounds to CPA, without treating CPA as a complete measure of generated-response quality.
items.title: Statistical Learning Theory for Direct Preference Optimization

items.summary: Evaluating an agent's planning ability remains challenging for open-domain tasks, where verifying procedures through execution is often impractical. Existing evaluations typically assess only the final plan and do not distinguish procedural errors such as missing, incorrect, or misordered actions. We introduce STEPBENCH, a benchmark of 6,885 verified procedures crawled from wikiHow across 81 open-domain categories. From each procedure, we derive 5 diagnostic tasks: four with deterministic answers involving withheld, incorrect, or shuffled steps, and one requiring next-step generation. We additionally evaluate full-plan generation to examine how diagnostic performance correlates with end-to-end plan validity. Using the same procedures across tasks lets us directly compare different planning capabilities. For generation, STEPEVAL identifies critical failures that prevent goal completion. Across 14 configurations of 12 models, we find substantial differences across planning capabilities, with step ordering proving the most difficult: the strongest model correctly orders only 63.0% of procedures, dropping to 33.1% for those with nine or more steps. Incorrect-step detection also predicts judged plan validity across models, suggesting a lower-cost alternative for evaluating generation quality. On STEPBENCH-Val, comprising 214 procedures published in 2026, comprehension scores and rankings remain stable, suggesting limited influence from memorisation.
items.title: StepBench: Diagnosing Real-World Procedural Understanding in AI Agents

items.summary: Long-running agents rely on memory of their past interactions for task state, such as what has been completed and which conditions still hold. Such state is usually a derived state. No record states it, and it must be computed by rules from multiple records of an evolving history. Existing memory benchmarks score only the final answer, with no reference for the intermediate states behind it. A wrong answer therefore cannot be traced to the state that was missed, and a state that silently became outdated goes undetected. We present MemDerive, a diagnostic benchmark for agent memory over evolving data. It specifies each scenario symbolically, derives exact gold answers with Datalog, records the gold derivation DAG and the supporting events of every query, and renders the history in natural language with fictional entities and distractors. Its 10 scenarios contain 4,692 events and 1,503 queries whose difficulty varies along access, evolution, and composition. On this ground truth, MemDerive evaluates answer reliability, diagnoses failures by probing the nodes of the gold derivation DAG, and tracks whether answers stay correct as events arrive. Our evaluation of four memory systems reveals failures that final-answer benchmarks hide. On derived state, every memory system falls behind simple BM25 retrieval, although the same answer model reaches 96.01% when given the supporting events. Most failures are ungathered, as a system holds the missing intermediate state but does not retrieve it for the question that needs it. Memory systems also rarely propagate implicit changes, which no new record states. These results suggest three principles for memory design. Gather inputs along the derivation, store rules with their versions, and maintain derived states through recorded dependencies.
items.title: MemDerive: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Agent Memory over Evolving Data

items.summary: World models are increasingly judged by how well they rank plausible futures, yet plausibility alone is the wrong target. The same scene can evolve under many latent rules, and a future that is smooth and physically valid under one rule can be incoherent under the rule actually in force. We formalize the resulting failure, operator-blindness, and show that it is systematically hidden by standard evaluation: a scorer can attain near-perfect generic ranking while separating current-world from other-world futures no better than chance. We introduce Operator-Mismatch Contrastive (OMC) learning, whose semantic hard negatives are valid-but-wrong-operator trajectories, and a matching protocol that measures world-relative coherence directly. On a controlled synthetic benchmark with in- and out-of-distribution operator parameters, across two trajectory-scoring backbones, and on feature-level external validation with CoPhy ballsCF, OMC raises operator-sensitive scoring far above a chance baseline that nonetheless achieves 0.99 generic top-1. We prove that the wrong-operator negative is necessary both for the protocol to detect the failure and for the objective to fix it, and position OMC as an auxiliary coherence signal (a trajectory-coherence scorer, not a generative model, planner, or control agent) that can be attached to existing world-model representations.
items.title: Operator-Mismatch Contrastive Learning for World-Relative Trajectory Coherence

items.summary: Long videos often exceed the context capacity of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), while agentic search repeats costly video processing and grounding for each query. Reusable memory can amortize this cost, but must preserve information for questions unknown during construction. We propose Video-EMem, an evolvable video memory harness built on time-anchored perceptual observations. This representation combines compact free-form text with sparse images to preserve semantic content and complementary visual details across temporal scales, supporting temporal navigation without a fixed semantic schema. A Writer encodes each video once by consolidating overlapping multiscale observations, and a Reader retrieves and organizes evidence solely from the resulting memory. With the underlying models frozen, we evolve their workflows and operators using distinct feedback: query-independent source fidelity and coverage for the Writer, and QA failures in evidence localization and utilization for the Reader. Experiments support this separation for generalization beyond development queries, with our evolution strategy improving average accuracy by 7.2% over the unevolved harness. While reducing storage by about 99.86% on average relative to raw videos, Video-EMem improves Qwen3-VL-30B by an average of 2.6% across three long-video QA benchmarks over direct input of 2,048 frames. Using the same o3 answer model as the state-of-the-art agentic method, it improves average accuracy by 2.5% with lower per-query latency.
items.title: Write Once, Query Many: Evolving Compact Reusable Memory for Long Videos

items.summary: As model reasoning gets cheaper, the physical experiment becomes the slow and costly step in discovery. Each experiment returns a noisy reading: a high value can mean a good candidate or a lucky draw. With a fixed budget, an AI agent must keep choosing between exploring a new candidate and confirming a promising one by re-testing it. We measure that choice in Wellocate, a simulated assay campaign with known true values. It is built on a generated landscape and on two real protein datasets, GB1 and PhoQ, scrambled so no model can answer from memory. We test five language models as minimal agents, with no tools and no memory beyond the history in each prompt. They misallocate in both directions. Three over-confirm, spending most of the budget re-testing. On the generated landscape one under-confirms, trusting single readings, and there every model ends with a worse final pick than a basic scripted strategy. Each failure has its own cause. The over-confirmers run short of new candidates worth trying: a list of untried candidates cuts their re-testing and, on real protein data, makes two of them pick much better. A running summary of their readings or a description of the landscape changes it by at most five percentage points. For the under-confirmer, re-testing its top candidates in a final round, replayed on its own campaigns, recovers only about a quarter of what it loses by picking the wrong candidate. This suggests confirmation has to run through the whole campaign. We release Wellocate as a benchmark and reinforcement-learning environment with frozen splits and scripted baselines. With it, anyone can measure how an agent splits its budget before trusting it with real experiments, and train agents to split it better. Code, data and the environment are available at https://github.com/Xstendyl/wellocate.
items.title: Explore or Confirm? LLM Agents Misallocate Measurements Under Noise

items.summary: Sea Surface Temperature, Wave Height and Period Measurement Details: 16 offshore, coastal and inshore moored buoys with on-board data loggers and telemetry via GOES; onboard calculation of significant wave height and peak period. Various starting dates, beginning as early as 1988. Publication: "Technical details on data processing, calibration etc are available in ""Meteorological and Oceanographic Measurements from Canadian Weather Buoys - a Review of Sensors, Data Reduction, Transmission, Quality Control and Archival Methods"", 1996. Prepared by Axys Environmental Consulting Ltd. for Environment Canada. Copy in IOS Library Technical Records." Real-time data are received at IOS and eventually replaced by data from AES that has been through their QC/QA procedures. PSARC_Utility: Data are archived at their original sampling interval (hourly). There have been subjected to AES quality control, but there are gaps in the data due to sensor or system failures. items.title: Offshore Meteorological/Oceanographic Buoys - Canada - FGDC XML metadata artifact

items.summary: Robotic value models assess task execution from visual observations and instructions, providing feedback for policy learning and execution monitoring. However, existing evaluations cover only selected aspects of execution understanding, leaving the reliability of value feedback insufficiently tested. We introduce RoboValue, a fine-grained sim-and-real benchmark for unified evaluation of robotic value models. Its framework evaluates four complementary capability dimensions through shared interfaces: task-state understanding, temporal progress monitoring, failure and recovery reasoning, and value consistency. Diagnostic trajectories and instruction variations test whether value judgments accurately reflect task requirements and changes throughout execution. RoboValue-Dataset covers 15 simulation and 20 real-world manipulation tasks, providing expert demonstrations for training and annotated trajectories for fine-grained evaluation. We evaluate representative robotic value models in zero-shot and one-shot settings under standard conditions and separate shifts in robot embodiment and environment. Our results reveal errors in fine-grained instruction grounding, history-dependent progress tracking, and recovery assessment, even in models with strong outcome and forward-progress scores. The same semantic subtask can also receive substantially different value gains across valid execution orders. These findings identify concrete targets for value supervision, while the dataset and public leaderboard support continued assessment of feedback reliability. The website is available at https://robovalue-benchmark.github.io/.
items.title: RoboValue: A Fine-Grained Sim-and-Real Benchmark for Unified Evaluation of Robotic Value Models

items.summary: Language models increasingly use skills that provide reusable instructions and procedures for task execution. After a relevant skill has been selected, the model may need to apply its governing procedure together with retrieved task context. When the retrieved context is useful but contains cues that violate the skill, the model must retain compatible information while rejecting the conflicting cues. We study failures in which the model adopts such cues and produces a retrieval-supported but skill-invalid answer, which we call procedural hallucination. We introduce SourceClash, a matched benchmark with 1,271 bundles and 6,355 prompts across ten procedural domains. Each bundle fixes the task, skill specification, and answer space while varying the relation between the skill and retrieval. Across nine models, valid-answer rates average 25.7% under conflicting retrieval, compared with 78.2% and 72.8% under two supportive retrieval settings. Mechanistic analysis of open-weight models shows that the answer-preference difference typically reaches its maximum shortly after generation begins. Residual replacement moves the model toward valid answers, while attention decomposition attributes most of the repair to value vectors. Intervention at the identified value pathway also improves final answer validity. These results characterize how partly conflicting retrieval changes skill-guided generation.
items.title: When Retrieval Partially Conflicts with Skills: Understanding Procedural Hallucination in Language Models

items.summary: Modeling cascading failure across interdependent critical infrastructure requires either a composable physical simulator per domain or a topological abstraction that discards quantity awareness. Simulators are costly, data-hungry, and require detailed calibration per domain; topological abstractions stay data-parsimonious while missing quantity-based behaviors that govern real dynamics. We present, instead, a knowledge-driven propagation architecture in which heterogeneous service dependencies are identified by categories: a general logical propagation resolves multi-dependency and redundancy structures purely from how nodes are categorized, while quantity-aware categories plug in dedicated mechanisms - here, a max-min fair-share flow module for water distribution. Both share one discrete functionality scale and a monotonic update algorithm guaranteeing convergence in finitely many rounds. We assess the flow module by comparing its results with those we get from preexisting pressure-driven simulation with WNTR (Water Network Tool for Resilience) on eight realistic networks across four failure families (clustered damage, capacity-targeted attack, source failure, tank loss). Under capacity-targeted attack and source failure a topological-reachability baseline misses 46% of the truly critical junctions, where the flow module misses 10% and 8% at an average critical-class precision of 0.73. Supplementary materials, code and results are available at: https://github.com/cascade-platform-org/CASCADE
items.title: Composable, Knowledge-Driven Disservice Propagation for Complex Interdependent Services with a Flow-Allocation Module Validated Against Hydraulic Simulation

items.summary: Biogenic nutrient (nitrate, nitrite, ammonium, phosphate and silicate) and Phytoplankton chlorophyll data were collected from CTD/rossette casts on selected SEBSCC cruises on the SE Bering Sea shelf. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.
items.title: SEBSCC Nutrient and Chlorophyll Data - FGDC XML metadata artifact

items.summary: AI agents deployed inside organizations can pose an insider threat if they make mistakes, are compromised by an attacker, or pursue misaligned objectives. We propose honeypots as an AI control method to improve the security of internal agent deployments. Rather than only using honeypots for pre-deployment evaluations, defenders should plant decoy opportunities for harmful actions throughout the production environment to detect misbehavior, incriminate malicious agents, and deter attacks. Such honeypots can elicit misbehavior under real deployment conditions, identify malicious agents even if chain-of-thought monitorability degrades, provide reliable warnings about agent misbehavior to security teams, and scale cheaply to many agent instances. The presence of honeypots also introduces uncertainty about which opportunities are real, thus deterring malicious agents from attacking and reducing the rate of misbehavior. We discuss the limitations of honeypots and give reasons to expect them to remain effective as agent capabilities increase. Finally, we outline key research questions to measure and improve the effectiveness of honeypots: testing the robustness of honeypots, comparing their detection effectiveness with other monitoring methods, understanding their incrimination and deterrence effects, and building supporting infrastructure.
items.title: Honeypots for AI Agent Insider Threats

items.summary: We investigate quantum-state texture during the thermal relaxation of an anisotropic spin-$1/2$ Heisenberg dimer subject to a longitudinal magnetic field and a Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction. Starting from local transverse and longitudinal couplings to a bosonic bath, we construct a global weak-coupling Lindblad equation, identify its transition channels, and discuss the applicability and limitations of the secular approximation. The Gibbs state is obtained explicitly in the local spin basis, revealing that the DM coupling controls both the modulus and phase of the single-excitation coherence by modifying the energy splitting and rotating the chiral phase. For heating and cooling protocols, we compare rugosity, fidelity-based texture, and trace-distance texture with coherence, vector spin chirality, and purity. The relaxation dynamics separates population thermalization from the decay and precession of deliberately prepared energy-basis coherence. Their combined contribution to local coherence produces DM-dependent texture overshoots and, during cooling, damped oscillations and sign changes of the coherence quadratures. These transients differ from the evolution of coherence magnitude and purity, while trace-distance texture weights them differently from the overlap-based quantifiers. Calculations at reduced dissipation preserve the texture maxima within the secular model. The results identify a phase-sensitive diagnostic of relaxation.
items.title: Phase-sensitive quantum-state texture during thermalization of a Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya Heisenberg dimer

items.summary: engiNIR 1.0.0, the first public release. Install with uv add enginir or pip install enginir (Python 3.12 or newer). Documentation: https://enginir.readthedocs.io First public release. Workflow enginir.Project runs the project workflow in one call per step: add_dataset , add_target , Dataset.add_roi , fit and Model.predict , with datasets, ROIs, targets and models addressed by name. Calibrations, sample sets, signal domains, stored recipes and provenance are created automatically. One HDF5 project file (schema viewer-v3 ) holds datasets, calibrations, ROIs, reference values, preprocessing recipes, signal domains, sample sets, model runs and prediction runs, linked by stable ids. Desktop viewer enginir-viewer with the Explore, Model and Predict workspaces, built on the same Project rules. Library Readers for EVK EIFF, ENVI, HDF5, CSV/Excel, SPC, SPA and JCAMP-DX. Preprocessing: Savitzky-Golay smoothing and derivatives, SNV, MSC, EMSC, detrending and smoothing, as scikit-learn transformers and as validated PreprocessingRecipe s. Models: PLS and PCR for the project workflow; SIMCA, LDA, SVR, random forest and MLP as scikit-learn estimators. Validation: grouped cross-validation, Kennard-Stone, RMSEC/RMSECV/RMSEP, R², bias, RPD and RPIQ, leverage, Hotelling T² and Q outliers. Plots of spectra, predictions, scores, loadings, VIP and image maps. Guarantees Training and prediction convert and preprocess spectra with the same code; MSC and EMSC are fitted inside every cross-validation fold. Cross-validation groups by ROI, so pixels of one ROI never appear in both training and validation folds. Prediction is refused before it runs when the data cannot produce the model's signal (instrument format, number of bands, calibration, signal unit). Every object is validated when it is written and when a project is opened; stored objects cannot be overwritten with different content. Prediction streams through image files in bounded memory. Packaging Python 3.12 and newer; CI runs on 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14. Install from PyPI with uv add enginir or pip install enginir . Documentation on Read the Docs: https://enginir.readthedocs.io . Each GitHub release is archived on Zenodo and uploaded to PyPI by a workflow that checks that the tag matches the version and that CI passed for the commit. Notes for users of pre-1.0 versions Fitted estimators pickled with engiNIR before 1.0 cannot be loaded: their fitted state means something else (the PLS intercept, for example, applied to mean-centred spectra) and would give wrong predictions. Loading one raises an error; fit the model again. Pickles now record the engiNIR version. SNV divides by the sample standard deviation (n - 1), as defined by Barnes et al.; earlier versions used the population standard deviation, which scales SNV spectra by sqrt(n / (n - 1)) (0.2 % for 220 bands). Release candidates 1.0.0rc1 to 1.0.0rc3 were tagged but not published; 1.0.0rc4 was published as a pre-release. The library code is the same in all release candidates and in 1.0.0; they differ in tests, packaging and documentation only.
items.title: engiNIR: A universal engineering tool for near-infrared spectra and hyperspectral imaging

items.summary: Code, job scripts and derived results supporting a study of operational water level forecasting for flood monitoring in Lamphun, northern Thailand. Five compact single-hidden-layer neural networks forecast hourly stage 6 to 18 hours ahead at three gauges (P.5, P.87, P.85), each paired with an upstream gauge. The record contains the open-source NumPy (Levenberg–Marquardt) ANN on which all retrospective results are based, evaluated on 65 leave-one-flood-year-out blocks (configurations from an earlier MATLAB experiment published separately); benchmarks against persistence, a linear model given the same inputs, XGBoost, and long short-term memory (LSTM) and GRU networks with a sensitivity analysis; leakage checks (predictor selection by LASSO repeated inside every block, whole-year early stopping, an antecedent-rainfall candidate pool); Diebold–Mariano tests, a datum-independent Kling–Gupta efficiency, threshold exceedance scores, skill by flow state, upstream travel time and a scan for frozen gauge records; and the reference code and a 76-day evaluation (2 August–17 October 2026) of the deployed hourly forecasting and alerting service. Summary results for every table and figure are included, with a synthetic example dataset that demonstrates the input format and evaluation code. The hourly water levels and daily rainfall were obtained from the Royal Irrigation Department (RID), Thailand, and are not included because redistribution permission has not been confirmed; with those data, the retrospective analyses can be re-run from the scripts provided. The record supports a manuscript and does not constitute validation of an autonomous flood-warning system.   Supports the manuscript submitted to *Natural Hazards*: *Selecting hourly water-level forecasting models for flood warning in small-to-medium basins of Thailand: benchmarks, leakage control and operational verification*. Every retrospective result is based on the open-source Python ANN (P.87 with 5 hidden units), with leakage checks and a 76-day operational record. - New analysis code: `python_main_evaluation.py`, `model_comparison.py` (all methods on the hours common to every method; Table 2, Fig. 3), `gbm_benchmark.py` (XGBoost), `infold_selection.py` (in-fold LASSO; base, causal-wavelet and rainfall pools; Table 3), `rain_daily_parse.py` (daily-rainfall parser; rainfall not included), `export_travel_time_data.py` and `export_travel_time_py.py` (Fig. 5 values), `rain_delta_rmse.py` (per-year rainfall effect), `gbm_tuned.py` and `gbm_tuned_eval.py` (nested-tuned XGBoost), `swrm_additions.py` (90% prediction intervals, P.87 one-unit check, P.85 bias and stage relation), `code/ann/python/ann_rerun.py` (5 hidden units for P.87; whole-year early stopping). - GRU: `lstm_benchmark.py` updated (`--cell gru`) and `hpc/slurm/gru_erawan.sbatch` added. - New results: `python_main_evaluation.json`, `model_comparison.json` and per-year CSVs, `gbm_runs.json`, `gru_benchmark.json`, `infold_selected_*.json`, `rain_delta_rmse_per_year.csv`, `gbm_tuned_runs.json`, `gbm_tuned_eval.json`, `swrm_additions.json`, `operational_evaluation_20261017.json` (window to 17 October 2026), per-year metrics of the ANN reruns. - `figures/`: the eight figures of the Natural Hazards manuscript (Fig1–Fig8); earlier figures remain in versions 1.0.0 and 1.1.0. - Removed: the MATLAB reference scripts with their registry builder and MATLAB-vs-Python comparison files (published separately by T. Chaipimonplin; `registry.json` is kept), and all figure-drawing scripts (the record ships the final figures only). - Environment: scikit-learn 1.7.1, xgboost 3.4.1, scipy 1.16.1 added.
items.title: Lamphun Flood Forecasting: Analysis Code and Evaluation Results

items.summary: Frontier LLMs can copy random text almost flawlessly, yet they often overrun or truncate long blocks of repeated characters. In repeated strings, matching local content no longer reliably identifies where copying should continue or when it should stop. Nevertheless, we show that a two-layer transformer with $O(\log\log N)$-bit precision and $O(\log N/\log\log N)$ width can copy every string up to a chosen design horizon $N$ and terminate correctly under arbitrary repetition. We use RoPE-style rotations of attention values and outputs (VO-rotations) with small prime periods to encode distances from delimiter anchors modulo those primes. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, these periodic encodings jointly distinguish all required distances, allowing one retrieval rule to select either the next source token or the end marker. In contrast, we prove a width-independent impossibility result for copying under sequential finite-precision softmax accumulation. It applies to transformers whose only positional input is an additive attention bias that eventually becomes constant, including NoPE and a recursive implementation of ALiBi. Once an identical-token run exceeds the resulting saturation threshold, further repetitions leave the logits unchanged. If this threshold grows sublinearly with $N$, these models cannot both complete a long all-identical copy and stop correctly, a pattern resembling the termination errors of frontier LLMs. In synthetic copying experiments, baseline transformer models fail on long repeated strings even within the training range. Trained VO models, by contrast, generalize beyond the training lengths with near-perfect accuracy up to length $\approx 5005$, the selected primes' period product.
items.title: Copying Under Repetition: From Prefix Matching to Position Hashing

items.summary: Example data to reproduce the BAGFOOT2 protocol and vignette: mouse liver ATAC-seq, Fed vs Fasted (3 replicates per condition, mm10). BAGFOOT2 predicts which transcription factors change their activity between two conditions from ATAC-seq data, by combining Tn5 bias-corrected footprint depth and flanking accessibility over archetype motif clusters, with a robust Mahalanobis distance (MCD) test. Files bam_merged.tar.gz: one merged, sorted and indexed BAM file per condition (fed, fasted) bam_replicates.tar.gz: one BAM file per replicate (fed_1-3, fasted_1-3), used for HOMER (large file) tag_directories.tar.gz: HOMER tag directories of the replicates (TD_fed_1 ... TD_fasted_3) macs2.tar.gz: MACS2 peak calls (narrowPeak) per condition bg_files_fed_fasted.tar.gz: BAGFOOT2 (v2.0.0) output for Fed vs Fasted (bagplot, D2 and FDR barplots, result table) The motif database files (mm10, hg38) are NOT in this record. They are downloaded automatically by BAGFOOT2 on first use, from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20782782 How to reproduce Install BAGFOOT2: conda create -n bagfoot2 -c goldsteinlab-tech -c conda-forge -c bioconda bagfoot2 Extract the archives into one project folder: fed_fasted/bam_merged/ (merged BAM files, replicate BAM files and tag directories) fed_fasted/macs2/ (peak files) Run: bagfoot2 -b fed_fasted/bam_merged/ -p fed_fasted/macs2/ -o bg_files_fed_fasted/ -c fed -t fasted -g mm10 --bam_suffix ".sorted.bam" --cores 4 Add --homer TRUE --homer_bin /path/to/homer/bin --reps_control 1,2,3 --reps_treatment 1,2,3 to include HOMER motif enrichment. Code: https://github.com/goldsteinlab-tech/BAGFOOT2 Documentation: https://goldsteinlab-tech.github.io/BAGFOOT2/ RELATED WORKS Is supplement to: https://github.com/goldsteinlab-tech/BAGFOOT2 (Software) References: 10.5281/zenodo.20782782 (Dataset, motif database)

items.summary: We ask how much an autoregressive transformer retains of its prompt after generating $t$ tokens. Consider two different prompts followed by the same continuation text, so that any difference in their hidden states comes from the prompt alone, and we find that the distance between their hidden states decays approximately as a power law $t^{-α}$, where $α=1$ is the rate at which a fixed prompt's share of uniform attention shrinks and smaller values mean longer memory. Trained models forget fast ($α\approx0.55$--$0.7$), untrained ones slowly ($α\approx0.2$--$0.5$). We prove that this offset is $O\big(P(\log t)^{L-1}/t\big)$ for a prompt of length $P$ and depth $L$. The bound holds for finite-depth pre-LN softmax transformers with bounded attention logits, under one additional condition: the pre-norm activations stay away from zero. The mechanism is geometric: the prompt's direct influence is diluted as the context grows, and \emph{relay} --- continuation tokens passing on what earlier tokens read from the prompt --- can only add logarithmic factors. This is what we call the \emph{conditional no-hair theorem}: given the text generated so far, the prompt's influence on the next token vanishes as $t$ grows, so any property of the prompt that survives, such as its language, must be carried by the text itself. An exactly solvable linear relay model shows that the bound cannot be improved and reproduces the rise of the local exponent towards $1$ seen in untrained networks. Cancelling the dilution with a logit bias stops the decay early in training and reverses it after, so dilution is necessary for the forgetting we measure; untrained networks and the solvable model show it is also sufficient.
items.title: A Conditional No-Hair Theorem for Transformers: How Language Models Forget Their Prompt
